still_true: Wegovy's US list price is still $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
The FDA has approved no generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US; generic liraglutide is still the only generic incretin on the US market.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, and the oral Wegovy starting dose still costs $149 a month there.

The September 2027 tri-agency guidance allowing up to 30% premium differentials tied to verified adherence still stands, Illinois's ban on adherence-conditioned premiums is still the only state ban in force, and the suicidal-ideation warning is still off the labels.
The April 2033 Section 232 tariff of 100% on finished peptide drugs and peptide APIs from China and India is still in force, along with India's export-licence checks on direct-to-consumer shipments.

population.note: FICTIONAL. Cycling arithmetic: 42.0% ever-used − 32.3% current = 9.7% of adults who used and are off now. About 50% of current users are on a second or later course (16.15 points), and 3.4 points have cycled and are off again, including people partway through a deliberate drug holiday. So (16.15 + 3.4) / 42.0 ≈ 46.5% of ever-users have cycled. The other 6.3 points stopped once and have not restarted, down from 7.3 because the 2036 Medicare and Medicaid benefit pulled some of them back. Persistence and restart rates are carried over from 2034: roughly one-third at one year on cash weekly and oral products, ~60% on clinic-administered monthly MariTide and inside conditioned tracks, and 36–47% restarting within a year. Ever-use rose 7.4 points (~20.5M people), mostly over-65s and Medicaid adults entering through the new benefit. Age check (weights 0.20/0.32/0.24/0.24): 3.6 + 9.92 + 10.08 + 8.64 ≈ 32.3. Income thirds average 32.3. Users: 32.3% of ~277M adults ≈ 89.5M. FICTIONAL payer mix: Medicare 23.0M (25.7%: 14.6M on pre-existing comorbidity and AUD codes plus 8.4M on the new obesity benefit; ~20.8M of them are 65+ and ~2.2M are under-65 disabled); Medicaid 9.5M (10.6%: ~4.8M on the new weight-loss coverage, ~1.1M on the AUD label, the rest diabetes and other codes); commercial 19.0M (21.2%, ~10.6M of them in conditioned tracks); legitimate cash 28.0M (31.3%, including ~6.5M on the $149 TrumpRx starting dose indefinitely and ~2.6M on calm/focus plans); non-FDA-approved product 10.0M (11.2%: ~3.0M on 503B-compounded amycretin or MariTide-substitute regimens under shortage rules, ~7.0M on imported, 'research-peptide', counterfeit or re-filled product). Sum: 23.0 + 9.5 + 19.0 + 28.0 + 10.0 = 89.5. Public payers cover 32.5M (36%), and Medicare is now the largest single payer. 65+: ~66.5M × 36% ≈ 23.9M users, of whom ~3.1M pay through cash, retiree or employer plans, or the gray market. The bottom third rose 17.5 → 27 because of mandatory Medicaid weight-loss coverage, dual-eligibles and the regrown gray market. About 18% of adults have obesity and have never used a drug, concentrated among uninsured working-age adults in non-expansion Southern states, people who lost Medicaid to work-requirement churn, and people who refuse the drug. Adult obesity ~30.5%. Pediatric: 2.1% of under-18s are on a drug (~3.9% of 12–17s, ~0.8% of 6–11s), and ~62% of 6–11 starts are Medicaid/CHIP under EPSDT. About 5.9M children live with a parent who has regained after stopping.

access.public_coverage: FICTIONAL. Under the Medicare and Medicaid Obesity Treatment provisions of the July 2035 health package (federal statute, not state action), Medicare covers anti-obesity incretins from Jan 2036. Eligibility is BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with a weight-related comorbidity. Continuation requires ≥5% loss at six months and then maintenance of that loss, and any fill or administration gap over 60 days needs a new prior authorisation. Orals and self-injectables are paid under Part D. Clinic-administered monthly MariTide is paid under Part B at 20% coinsurance, usually picked up by Medigap. Statutory negotiated ceilings: $190/month for the obesity benefit, and a blended ~$210 for existing-code users after the 2035 renegotiation. Medicare arithmetic: 14.6M × $210 × 12 ≈ $36.8B, plus 8.4M × $190 × 12 ≈ $19.2B, gives ≈ $56.0B gross annual incretin spend (up from ~$38.3B). CBO's 10-year score for the obesity benefit assumed uptake plateauing near 10M at falling prices: 10M × ~$170 × 12 ≈ $20.4B/yr, about $194B gross over 2036–2045 before offsets. Medicaid: the statute struck the optional weight-loss exclusion from Jan 2036, with 80% federal match for weight-loss use through FY2038. Arithmetic: 4.8M × ~$150 net × 12 ≈ $8.6B, of which states owe ≈ $1.7B. Adding the ~4.7M other-route users (4.7M × $150 × 12 ≈ $8.5B at regular match) gives ≈ $17.1B total Medicaid incretin spend. No state chose this. The two state programmes that condition coverage now apply the federal 5% rule. CMS's AUD coding audit closed in Oct 2035 and found ~22% of sampled Part D AUD diagnoses undocumented, leading to recoupments from three telehealth prescribers.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide is $4–28 a month inside India and in 100+ export markets. Chinese tirzepatide-analogue vials are $18–55, and a China-approved monthly semaglutide microsphere depot (approved 2035) is ~$70 a month there. Canadian and Brazilian generics are CAD 40–75 and BRL 150–260. Delivered to US addresses, tariffed Indian or Chinese product costs ~$90–170, but product finished or relabelled in Mexico or Vietnam to dodge origin rules arrives at ~$60–120. India and China still supply roughly two-thirds of world incretin volume.
access.note: FICTIONAL. The 2035 TrumpRx round: Wegovy pill maintenance $179 (the starting dose stays at $149), Foundayo $149–199, injectable Wegovy/Zepbound $199–249, MariTide $229, oral amycretin listed at $299 (cash direct was ~$449), retatrutide $329. Branded cash now sits at $149–329, and access is rationed by coverage and prior authorisation, not by price. Business Group on Health (Nov 2036): 34% of employers cover weight-management use, ~70% of them with adherence or progress conditions. Several large employers dropped coverage for retirees 65+ and pointed them to Medicare. Route mix: orals ~50% of users (oral amycretin ~8.6M), weekly injectables ~33%, monthly MariTide ~17% (~15.5M, up from 5.8M; ~60% of them Medicare, and ~55% clinic-administered at CVS, Walgreens and Amgen-partnered infusion suites). The regrown gray market runs through three channels. First, 503B compounding of amycretin, legal while it sits on FDA's shortage list since Mar 2036, sold by telehealth platforms at $99–159. Second, 'research-use' retatrutide and cagrilintide-semaglutide vials routed through Mexican and Vietnamese finishing to evade the 2033 tariff. Third, the domestic re-filling that started in 2033.

GLP-1/amylin unimolecular co-agonist, daily oral (oral amycretin)

GLP-1 agonist/GIP-receptor antagonist antibody conjugate, monthly injectable (maridebart cafraglutide: MariTide), now including a monthly self-administered autoinjector (Sep 2035) and every-8-week maintenance dosing

pediatric obesity ages 6–11 (liraglutide incl. generics; weekly semaglutide), with growth-velocity, Tanner and eating-disorder screening language

physician-directed dose-downs below label maintenance to relieve flatness
'calm' and 'focus' low-dose plans (~2.6M), now marketed as 'dose-down' and 'gentle' plans

semaglutide in 12–14-year-olds at doses above label titration in gray channels
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. No new indication was approved in this window. Lilly resubmitted tirzepatide for dementia-risk reduction in adults 60+ without CVD in Mar 2035. An advisory committee voted 9–5 against in Jan 2036, citing the hip-fracture excess in women 70+, and FDA issued a complete response letter in Mar 2036. The monthly driver is realised through an existing product in new forms. Amgen's sBLA for a self-administered MariTide monthly autoinjector, filed Aug 2034, was approved Sep 2035, together with every-8-week maintenance dosing for patients stable for 12 months. Clinic administration under Part B made the monthly injection the default for Medicare starters. Subdermal implants (a semaglutide device and a tirzepatide device) are still in phase 2. One sponsor began a phase 3 in mid-2036, and no implant is on the US market. Novo's monthly injectable semaglutide-analogue is in phase 2. No oral exceeds amycretin's ~21.5%, and none matches retatrutide's ~24%. Global incretin market ~$228B (2035): volume up, net price down. US branded net prices fell ~8% in 2035–36 through Medicare ceilings and the TrumpRx round.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation outside clinic tracks. MariTide's first-dose vomiting is the main reason Medicare starters miss month two. Chronic diarrhoea is routinely worked up for EPI.

safety_ledger.effect: Gastroparesis, ileus and bowel obstruction (persistent delayed gastric emptying)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Whether gastroparesis persists after stopping is still disputed. The first two MDL bellwether trials split in 2035: a defence verdict in October, then a $14M plaintiff verdict in December against Novo, which is on appeal. GI claims passed ~46,000. No new cohort signal.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No new labelling; settlement talks under a court-appointed mediator.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss; unchanged. Medicare cholecystectomy volume rose with the 2036 starters, roughly in line with labelled rates.
Still no causal confirmation for acute pancreatitis; absolute risk low.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Medicare hip-fracture HR still ~1.3 after more than 2 years and ~1.45 after three or more cycles. The Medicare obesity benefit is putting several million first-time users over 65 on drug in a single year, and the fracture rates in that group will not be readable until 2037–38.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class warning retained. The Medicare benefit pays for a baseline DXA in 65+ starters but does not require one. Bimagrumab label unchanged.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Conflicting cohorts; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Listed in adverse reactions; no class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal in adults or in AUD-label users.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The 2033 FDA observational estimate stands: ~7% at maintenance doses vs ~3.5% of controls, ~10% on retatrutide. Rates at low doses and on monthly MariTide are still unmeasured. Complaints are now mainstream, but no new study has been reported.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No labelling change. FDA's 2035 Federal Register notice invited sponsors to propose dose-reduction studies, and none has been filed.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Half to two-thirds regain within 18 months, worse after repeated cycles. People on drug holidays regain ~1–2% per month off. Medicare continuation rules end coverage for those who regain below the 5% threshold.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly; it underpins the federal 5% continuation rule.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: B12, iron, vitamin D and, in AUD-label users who keep drinking, thiamine deficiency. Low ferritin in adolescent girls. Protein-calorie shortfall is now reported in frail 65+ Medicare starters.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Annual micronutrient panel language retained; thiamine counselling on the AUD label.

safety_ledger.effect: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency after 5+ years of continuous use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: ~2× EPI incidence after more than 5 years of continuous semaglutide, and tirzepatide HR ~1.3. No new data changed this. Novo announced a ~$7.1B settlement framework for the EPI arm in Jun 2036, above its $6.2B reserve. The DOJ civil investigation is ongoing.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled for semaglutide and tirzepatide. Novo is under an FDA-supervised pharmacovigilance remediation plan.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; effects in children on drug for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About fourteen years of semaglutide follow-up exist. Cycling effects are still poorly characterised and now include patterned drug holidays. There are no data on indefinite starting-dose use or on 8-week MariTide maintenance beyond 2 years.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric bone and growth postmarketing requirements continue.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed ~39,000 as the gray market regrew. 503B amycretin dosing-conversion errors (oral-to-injectable mg confusion) drove a rise in poison-centre calls in 2036. Re-filled-vial infections continue at a lower rate than the 2034 Burkholderia cluster. This is the existing signal growing with volume, not a new mechanism.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA warning letters to 14 'research peptide' sellers, CBP origin-fraud cases against Mexican finishers, and a 2036 compounding-conversion safety communication. No statute changed and no state acted.

safety_ledger.effect: Growth deceleration, delayed puberty and restrictive eating in children started young
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Height velocity is still ~0.5–0.6 cm/year below expected in prepubertal starters, with partial catch-up after stopping. The Swedish ARFID HR is ~1.8. Final adult height is still unknown.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Monitoring language and medication guide, no REMS. AAP keeps lifestyle-first as the preferred approach for prepubertal children.

safety_ledger.effect: Alcohol-related harms on the AUD label (dehydration, alcoholic ketoacidosis, aspiration with vomiting during binge drinking)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Still ~1 per 2,000 person-years during titration; the postmarketing study is enrolling.

food_and_beverage.state: About half of US households now have a user, and in Medicare-heavy zips the share is higher. Snack and confectionery volume is down ~16% from 2025 and sugary drinks ~13%. Senior-skewed categories fell fastest in 2036: soft-baked cookies, ice cream pints, and the boxed-dessert aisle in Florida and Arizona. A small premium 'real food' segment (full-fat dairy, heritage bakery, butcher counters) grows in top-income zips, sold on appetite rather than restraint. It is too small to offset the volume loss, so dollar sales slipped again.

alcohol.state: Spirits volume is down ~20% from 2025 and beer ~13%. Medicare coverage reached heavy-drinking retirees. Kentucky barrel laydown is down again, and distributor consolidation continues. A niche 'unmedicated' craft and natural-wine scene in Brooklyn and Austin sells drinking as proof of appetite, but it is a rounding error in volume.

restaurants.state: Total traffic is down slightly. In Sarasota, Ocala and The Villages, buffet and early-bird traffic fell ~15% year over year after the Medicare benefit began, and two regional buffet chains closed Florida units. At the other end, long tasting menus and steakhouses in Manhattan, LA and Austin are booked out as status venues for visibly eating. QSR value menus still serve the uncovered.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking, and senior-catalogue retailers saw a size-down wave in 2036. Resale absorbs cyclers and holiday-takers. In upper-income menswear and women's tailoring, cuts are moving toward a fuller, muscled silhouette marketed against 'the drug look'.

fitness.state: Strength training keeps growing. Medicare Advantage plans bundle resistance classes with the obesity benefit to protect bone, which feeds SilverSneakers-type programmes. 'Natural' strength federations added incretin testing. Premium gyms sell 'unmedicated' cohorts.

insurance.state: Medicare is now the default payer for older users. The 2036 Part D base premium rose ~9%, and MA plans priced the benefit into supplemental tradeoffs. Employer coverage is 34%, about 70% of it conditioned. Some employers moved retirees to Medicare, and commercial pharmacy trend eased to ~+5%. Medicaid absorbed ~4.8M new weight-loss users under a federal mandate, and states' share is ~$1.7B a year until enhanced match ends in FY2038.

pharma.state: Volume is up and net price down. Amgen is the window's winner, because Part B clinic administration of MariTide matched what Medicare wanted. Novo carries the EPI settlement while oral amycretin sells out and lands on the shortage list. Lilly lost the dementia extension. 503B compounders and Mexican finishers took back share that the 2033 tariff had removed.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thin no longer signals much except who your payer is. A slow, soft, even loss in a 70-year-old reads as Medicare. Thin with a teenager's appetite at dinner reads as rich. 'Government thin' is the sneer of 2036, used on both coasts and in the Gulf states. The new scarce body is muscled, eats in public, and can prove it is unmedicated. A $79 direct-to-consumer incretin-free blood panel sells as a credential, and dating apps let users display a verified result.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The class line moved from thin versus fat to appetite versus suppression. Upper-income 25–45-year-olds in Austin, Brooklyn and Santa Monica display eating: second helpings, bread baskets, documented 'full plates'. Many of them are on a drug quietly and take holidays before visible dinners. Most new thinness is in Medicare and Medicaid, and the uncovered working-age South is where obesity is now most concentrated. Upper-income parents still refuse semaglutide for prepubertal children, and Medicaid children still make up most 6–11 starts.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: 'Full table' suppers spread from Bread Alone congregations to secular dinner clubs that ban pills at the table, with mixed honesty about it. At retirement communities in Florida the 4:30 dinner is shorter and quieter. Weddings now schedule the toast for the 'holiday weekend' crowd.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Profiles carry 'unmedicated (verified)', 'on a holiday' or 'MariTide, monthly' as tags. 'Eats with me' is a stated preference. Partners plan drug holidays around anniversaries and trips, so that both of them are hungry and both are present.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has become a luxury good and a political sign. Among the upper tier it is a performance of health. To MAHA parents it is a birthright. The left-populist 'hunger tax' language from 2033 has turned into complaints about Medicaid's 5% rule. The 'Let Them Grow' coalition has nothing to march against at the federal level and mostly runs school-board fights.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The measured figure is still ~7% clinically meaningful anhedonia at maintenance doses vs ~3.5% in controls (~10% on retatrutide). Self-report is far higher. In a 2036 Gallup panel, 44% of current users said the drug 'dulls' something they miss, and 38% had taken a deliberate drug holiday in the past year. Holidays cluster in oral cash users. Monthly MariTide users cannot take a dose back for 30 days, which they call 'the long month', and they ask for dose-downs or the 8-week schedule instead. Calm plans stalled at ~2.6M and rebranded as 'gentle'.
interior_life.framing: Mostly a side effect now: 'the flatness', 'the long month'. Clinicians call it dose-related blunting and manage it with dose-downs. Platforms that sold 'quiet the noise' now sell 'find your dose'. HR still calls it steadiness, quietly.
interior_life.effect_on_work: The 60-day gap rule in Medicare and in employer tracks made drug holidays a compliance calendar. The '59-day holiday' is common advice on forums, and benefits managers see clusters of lapses ending on day 58. About 10.6M employees are in conditioned tracks. EAP AUD pill programmes continue at trucking and warehousing firms. The two EEOC charges are still unresolved. Some creative agencies informally encourage holidays before pitch weeks.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Off' memoir has turned into 'holiday' writing, about the weekends people let themselves want things. A hit 2036 HBO comedy follows a retired couple in Ocala on opposite drug schedules. Stand-up about 'government thin' plays in both red and blue rooms. Sportsbook handle keeps falling in insured suburbs, and live-music venues continue to cut nights.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples sync or deliberately offset their holidays, and the clinic appointment has replaced the pill window as the date that structures the month for MariTide households. Therapists describe 'holiday couples', who are close for two weeks a quarter and flat in between.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Seniors became a pro-benefit constituency overnight, and both parties claim the 2035 law ahead of the 2036 election. The backlash split: MAHA leaders attack 'government thin', while Unmuted pushes for low-dose and monthly anhedonia studies. 'Sedated electorate' claims still lack turnout evidence, and 65+ turnout in the 2036 primaries was ordinary.

state.regulatory_posture: Federal, legislative and expansive on coverage; permissive on approvals but no new indications in the window; contradictory on supply. FDA's shortage listing legally opened compounding while CBP prosecutes origin fraud. No state legislature or agency acted, and Illinois's ban is still the only one.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: The July 2035 health package created the Medicare obesity benefit from Jan 2036, with statutory negotiated ceilings, and struck Medicaid's optional weight-loss exclusion, with 80% federal match through FY2038. States are now paying for coverage they never voted for. The 2027 tri-agency 30% guidance stands, and OPM's FEHB conditions continue.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The federal 5% rule writes conditioning into Medicare and Medicaid. Part B clinic-administration claims are themselves the adherence record, and Part D fill gaps over 60 days trigger a new PA automatically. Smart-bottle logs still flow to employer wellness vendors under consent, and benefit brokers still buy de-identified cohorts. CMS used telehealth AUDIT-C records in its 2035 AUD recoupments.
state.workforce_or_military: TRICARE follows the Medicare-style continuation rule for obesity use. The Army recruit oral pilot continues without expansion. FMCSA guidance still covers on-label AUD use and is silent on calm plans and drug holidays.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The 2033 tariff and India's export checks stand. A WTO panel on Beijing's complaint was established in 2035, with no ruling. Volume leaks through Mexican and Vietnamese finishing plants that relabel Chinese and Indian API, and CBP has opened origin-fraud cases. Demand from the Medicare launch outran Amgen's fill-finish capacity and Novo's amycretin API supply, and FDA shortage listings followed in Mar 2036.

events.event: TrumpRx posts a new price round: oral amycretin listed at $299 a month (from ~$449 cash), injectable Wegovy and Zepbound cut to $199–249, MariTide to $229, Wegovy pill maintenance to $179. The $149 starting dose is unchanged

Congress passes a health package creating Medicare coverage of anti-obesity incretins from Jan 2036, at negotiated ceilings near $190 a month with a 5%-at-six-months continuation rule, and striking Medicaid's weight-loss exclusion with 80% federal match; no state legislature votes on it

FDA approves Amgen's monthly self-injected MariTide autoinjector and every-8-week maintenance dosing; pharmacies open MariTide administration suites billed under Medicare Part B, and monthly users nearly triple to ~15.5 million by late 2036

FDA complete response letter rejects tirzepatide for dementia-risk reduction in adults 60+ without heart disease, citing hip fractures in older women in the confirmatory trial; Lilly says it will run a new trial

Two months into the Medicare benefit, FDA adds amycretin and the MariTide autoinjector to the drug shortage list. 503B compounders and telehealth platforms start selling amycretin injections at $99–159, while Mexican-relabelled 'research' retatrutide undercuts the 2033 tariff. The non-approved market regrows to about 10 million users
A $79 direct-to-consumer 'unmedicated' incretin panel passes 600,000 tests, two dating apps add verified badges, and a Gallup panel finds 38% of users took a deliberate drug holiday in the past year

open_tensions: Medicare is now the default payer for older Americans, which put several million first-time users over 65 on drug in a single year while the hip-fracture HR of ~1.3 still stands. The benefit pays for DXA scans but does not require them, and the fracture data for this group arrives after the 2036 election.

Compounded amycretin is legal only while it stays on the shortage list. When FDA delists it, about 3 million compounded users lose their legal supply in a single notice, many of them Medicaid-adjacent people who left the $149 starting dose. The tariff-era 'hunger tax' could repeat with a federal label on it.

Drug holidays are mainstream while the 60-day gap rule turns them into a compliance calendar. Monthly injections remove the weekly choice and also remove the ability to stop quickly. Low-dose and monthly anhedonia rates are still unmeasured, and no sponsor has filed a dose-reduction study.

Thinness now reads as a public-payer body and appetite as wealth. States owe ~$1.7B a year for Medicaid coverage they never chose, enhanced match ends in FY2038, and most of the 6–11-year-olds on semaglutide are Medicaid children whose adult height is still unknown.

prose.headline: Government Thin: Medicare Made Everyone Slim. Now the Rich Show Off What They Can Still Eat
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2036 nearly one American adult in three takes an incretin drug, close to ninety million people, and more than four in ten have tried one. The biggest change of the past two years is who pays. In July 2035 Congress did what it had refused to do for a decade. It made Medicare pay for weight-loss drugs, at a negotiated ceiling near $190 a month, and it required Medicaid to do the same with most of the bill sent to Washington until 2038. The benefit began in January. By December about twenty-three million Medicare beneficiaries were on a drug, and Medicare had become the largest single payer in the class.

The law came with a condition copied from the federal employee plan: lose five percent in six months or lose coverage, and never let the gap between doses run past sixty days. The arithmetic works for Washington. Medicare spends about $56 billion a year on these drugs, and prices keep falling. In the spring of 2035 the TrumpRx channel cut the new amycretin pill from $449 to $299 and the injectables to around $200. No brand is cheap, but none is out of reach for the insured. Access is rationed now by forms, not price.

The pill is still the most common way to take the drug, but the growth is in the monthly shot. Amgen's MariTide got a home autoinjector and an every-other-month maintenance schedule in September 2035. Pharmacies opened back-room suites where retirees get their monthly dose from a nurse and Medicare Part B pays. For the old, adherence has stopped being something they choose each week. It is an appointment, and the appointment is the record.

Demand outran supply. In March amycretin and the MariTide autoinjector went onto the federal shortage list, which made it legal for compounders to make amycretin. Telehealth sites sell it for about $120. Behind them, vials relabelled in Mexico slip past the 2033 tariff on Chinese and Indian peptides, and the unapproved market has grown back to about ten million people. When the shortage ends, three million of them lose their legal supply in a single notice.

Nothing new was approved. Lilly's attempt to sell tirzepatide as dementia prevention to healthy sixty-year-olds was rejected over broken hips in older women. No new safety signal appeared. The old ones remain: the pancreas, the bones, the slowed growth of children, and the flatness.

The flatness is now something people talk about at dinner. Most users say the drug dulls something they miss, and more than a third have taken a deliberate holiday from it. Forums trade advice on the 59-day holiday, which is one day short of the gap that ends coverage. Monthly users complain about the long month, the thirty days after a shot that they cannot take back.

Cheap thinness has lost its value. On both coasts the sneer is 'government thin'. Status in Austin, Brooklyn and Santa Monica belongs to bodies that are muscled, eat in public and can prove they are unmedicated. A $79 blood test for that has sold six hundred thousand kits, and dating apps show the result as a badge. Steakhouses and tasting menus are booked out. In Ocala and The Villages the early-bird buffets are closing.

The states pay a share of a Medicaid benefit no legislature voted for. The children on semaglutide are still mostly Medicaid children, and their adult height is still unknown. From a distance the country is thinner, older, calmer and paid for. Up close the month runs on a schedule.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Dolores Pruitt, sixty-eight, sets the kitchen timer for her pills, the blood-pressure one and the calcium, and does not set one for the other thing, because the other thing happens at the CVS on SW College Road at ten-fifteen, the second Tuesday.

She drives the Buick. In the back room there are four recliners and a poster of a woman lifting a kettlebell with her grandson. The nurse, Marisol, weighs her first. Seven point one percent since February.

"You're safe," Marisol says, meaning the six-month line.

The shot is cold, then nothing. Her Medigap plan pays the forty-nine dollars, and the receipt says PART B.

At bridge Carol is on the pill and on a holiday, eleven days, for her granddaughter's wedding in Savannah. Carol eats two lemon squares and says she can taste again. Carol says the word *taste* like a password. Dolores eats one, slowly, out of courtesy.

Her daughter Renée calls from Jacksonville. Renée's insurance dropped her, so she buys amycretin from a website for one hundred and nineteen dollars. It comes in a cooler bag with a syringe chart. "It says milligrams but it's units," Renée says. "Or the other way." Dolores tells her to read it twice.

At five the Golden Platter on 200 has a CLOSED sign and the chairs are up. She and Hal eat soup at home. Hal is not on anything. He says she looks like the lady in the poster. He means it kindly.

She sleeps fine. She dreams about nothing she can remember. Thirty days until the next one.

least_plausible_claims.quote: 503B compounding of amycretin, legal while it sits on FDA's shortage list since Mar 2036, sold by telehealth platforms at $99–159

rationale.badness: Against 2026, about 90M users, 10M on non-approved product, and ~39,000 adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product mean a materially harder society. Conditioning is written into Medicare and Medicaid (5% rule, 60-day gap, adherence records), and anhedonia is mainstream but unmeasured at low doses and on MariTide (epistemic). Inequality eases somewhat, since the bottom third rose to 27% via public coverage, but the uncovered working-age South and Medicaid children remain losers. Obesity falls and coverage widens, so this is a recognisably harder society, not one most readers would refuse to live in.

rationale.generativity: The Dolores Pruitt scene is concrete: the CVS back room, the 7.1% weigh-in, a Medigap receipt, Carol's holiday lemon squares, Renée's mg-versus-units confusion and the closed Golden Platter. A few lines explain rather than show, but the film is rich.

least_plausible_claims.quote: The non-approved market regrows to about 10 million users

No chain shows how compounders obtain API and scale under the 100% tariff and licence checks.
